questions.stem: A is a solution of tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid containing 4.90 g of H2SO4 per dm^3. B is a solution of sodium hydroxide of unknown concentration. A was put in the burette and titrated against 25.0 cm^3 portions of B using methyl orange as indicator. The burette readings (cm^3) were: Rough: final 25.00, initial 0.00; 1st: final 24.50, initial 0.00; 2nd: final 24.95, initial 0.50; 3rd: final 25.55, initial 1.00. (a)(i) Tabulate the burette readings and calculate the volume of A used in each titration. [3 marks] (ii) Calculate the average volume of A used, from the three accurate titrations. [2 marks] (iii) State the colour change at the end-point. [1 mark] (iv) Write a balanced equation for the reaction. [2 marks] (b) From your results and the information provided, calculate the: (i) concentration of A in mol dm^-3; [2 marks] (ii) concentration of B in mol dm^-3; [4 marks] (iii) concentration of B in g dm^-3; [2 marks] (iv) mass of sodium tetraoxosulphate(VI) formed in each titration. [2 marks] (c) Why should the burette be rinsed with A, and not with water, before it is filled? [2 marks] [H = 1.0, O = 16.0, Na = 23.0, S = 32.0]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Volumes of A (cm^3): rough 25.00; 24.50, 24.45, 24.55 (composite table with final, initial and volume rows, readings to 2 decimal places)
2 marks: (a)(ii) Average = (24.50 + 24.45 + 24.55)/3 = 24.50 cm^3
1 mark: (a)(iii) Yellow to orange
2 marks: (a)(iv) H2SO4(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) -> Na2SO4(aq) + 2H2O(l) (1 mark formulae, 1 mark balancing)
2 marks: (b)(i) Molar mass of H2SO4 = 98 g mol^-1; concentration = 4.90/98 = 0.0500 mol dm^-3
4 marks: (b)(ii) Moles of A = 0.0500 x 24.50/1000 = 1.225 x 10^-3 mol (1 mark); mole ratio A:B = 1:2 (1 mark); moles of B = 2.45 x 10^-3 mol (1 mark); concentration of B = 2.45 x 10^-3 x 1000/25.0 = 0.0980 mol dm^-3 (1 mark)
2 marks: (b)(iii) Molar mass NaOH = 40 g mol^-1; 0.0980 x 40 = 3.92 g dm^-3
2 marks: (b)(iv) Moles of Na2SO4 = moles of A = 1.225 x 10^-3 mol; mass = 1.225 x 10^-3 x 142 = 0.174 g
2 marks: (c) Water left in the burette would dilute A and lower its concentration, giving a larger titre; rinsing with A ensures its concentration is unchanged
questions.explanation: Titres: 25.00, 24.50, 24.45, 24.55 cm^3; average of the accurate titres = 24.50 cm^3. Methyl orange goes from yellow (in alkali) to orange at the end-point. H2SO4 + 2NaOH -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O. Concentration of A = 4.90/98 = 0.0500 mol dm^-3; moles of A used = 1.225 x 10^-3; moles of NaOH = 2 x that = 2.45 x 10^-3 in 25.0 cm^3, so B = 0.0980 mol dm^-3 = 3.92 g dm^-3. Mass of Na2SO4 per titration = 1.225 x 10^-3 x 142 = 0.174 g. Rinsing with A avoids dilution by water.

questions.stem: A is a solution of hydrochloric acid of unknown concentration. B is a solution containing 5.30 g of anhydrous sodium trioxocarbonate(IV), Na2CO3, per dm^3. A was put in the burette and titrated against 25.0 cm^3 portions of B using methyl orange as indicator. The burette readings (cm^3) were: Rough: final 24.20, initial 0.00; 1st: final 24.80, initial 1.00; 2nd: final 23.75, initial 0.00; 3rd: final 24.35, initial 0.50. (a)(i) Tabulate the burette readings and calculate the volume of A used in each titration. [3 marks] (ii) Calculate the average volume of A used, from the three accurate titrations. [2 marks] (iii) State the colour change at the end-point. [1 mark] (iv) State one precaution taken while using the pipette. [1 mark] (b) From your results and the information provided, calculate the: (i) concentration of B in mol dm^-3; [2 marks] (ii) concentration of A in mol dm^-3, given that the equation for the reaction is Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2; [4 marks] (iii) concentration of A in g dm^-3; [2 marks] (iv) volume of carbon(IV) oxide, measured at s.t.p., liberated in each titration. [2 marks] (c) Explain why phenolphthalein is not a suitable indicator for this titration. [3 marks] [H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0, Na = 23.0, Cl = 35.5; molar volume of a gas at s.t.p. = 22.4 dm^3]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Volumes of A (cm^3): rough 24.20; 23.80, 23.75, 23.85 (composite table with final, initial and volume rows, readings to 2 decimal places)
2 marks: (a)(ii) Average = (23.80 + 23.75 + 23.85)/3 = 23.80 cm^3
1 mark: (a)(iii) Yellow to orange (pink)
1 mark: (a)(iv) Any one: rinse pipette with B before use; read the meniscus at eye level; do not blow out the last drop; avoid air bubbles
2 marks: (b)(i) Molar mass Na2CO3 = 106 g mol^-1; 5.30/106 = 0.0500 mol dm^-3
4 marks: (b)(ii) Moles of B = 0.0500 x 25.0/1000 = 1.25 x 10^-3 mol (1 mark); moles of HCl = 2 x 1.25 x 10^-3 = 2.50 x 10^-3 mol (1 mark); concentration of A = 2.50 x 10^-3 x 1000/23.80 (1 mark) = 0.105 mol dm^-3 (1 mark)
2 marks: (b)(iii) 0.105 x 36.5 = 3.83 g dm^-3
2 marks: (b)(iv) Moles of CO2 = moles of Na2CO3 = 1.25 x 10^-3 mol; volume = 1.25 x 10^-3 x 22.4 = 0.0280 dm^3 (28.0 cm^3)
3 marks: (c) The reaction is between a strong acid and a weak base (the trioxocarbonate(IV)) (1 mark); the end-point is in the acidic range, which suits methyl orange (1 mark); phenolphthalein changes colour in the alkaline range (at the NaHCO3 stage), so it would give only about half the true titre (1 mark)
questions.explanation: Titres 24.20, 23.80, 23.75, 23.85 cm^3; average 23.80 cm^3. Concentration of B = 5.30/106 = 0.0500 mol dm^-3, so 25.0 cm^3 contains 1.25 x 10^-3 mol Na2CO3, which reacts with 2.50 x 10^-3 mol HCl. Concentration of A = 2.50 x 10^-3/(23.80/1000) = 0.105 mol dm^-3 = 3.83 g dm^-3. CO2 per titration = 1.25 x 10^-3 x 22.4 = 0.0280 dm^3. Methyl orange is used because the end-point of a strong acid-weak base titration is acidic; phenolphthalein would decolourise when only NaHCO3 had formed.

questions.stem: A is 0.100 mol dm^-3 hydrochloric acid. B is a solution made by dissolving 14.3 g of hydrated sodium trioxocarbonate(IV), Na2CO3.xH2O, in distilled water and making up to 1.00 dm^3. A was put in the burette and titrated against 25.0 cm^3 portions of B using methyl orange as indicator. The burette readings (cm^3) were: Rough: final 25.40, initial 0.00; 1st: final 25.00, initial 0.00; 2nd: final 24.95, initial 0.00; 3rd: final 25.05, initial 0.00. (a)(i) Tabulate the burette readings and calculate the volume of A used in each titration. [3 marks] (ii) Calculate the average volume of A used, from the three accurate titrations. [2 marks] (iii) What is the purpose of the rough titration? [1 mark] (iv) Why is a white tile placed under the conical flask? [1 mark] (b) Given that Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2, calculate the: (i) number of moles of HCl in the average titre; [2 marks] (ii) concentration of B in mol dm^-3; [3 marks] (iii) molar mass of Na2CO3.xH2O; [2 marks] (iv) value of x; [2 marks] (v) percentage by mass of water of crystallisation in the hydrated salt. [2 marks] (c) What is meant by the term 'efflorescence'? [2 marks] [H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0, Na = 23.0]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Volumes of A (cm^3): rough 25.40; 25.00, 24.95, 25.05 (composite table with final, initial and volume rows, readings to 2 decimal places)
2 marks: (a)(ii) Average = (25.00 + 24.95 + 25.05)/3 = 25.00 cm^3
1 mark: (a)(iii) To find the approximate end-point so that the accurate titrations can be done quickly, adding A dropwise near the end-point
1 mark: (a)(iv) To make the colour change at the end-point easy to see
2 marks: (b)(i) 0.100 x 25.00/1000 = 2.50 x 10^-3 mol
3 marks: (b)(ii) Moles of Na2CO3 = 2.50 x 10^-3/2 = 1.250 x 10^-3 mol (1 mark) in 25.0 cm^3 (1 mark); concentration = 1.250 x 10^-3 x 1000/25.0 = 0.0500 mol dm^-3 (1 mark)
2 marks: (b)(iii) Molar mass = mass concentration/molar concentration = 14.3/0.0500 = 286 g mol^-1
2 marks: (b)(iv) 106 + 18x = 286; 18x = 180; x = 10
2 marks: (b)(v) % water = (10 x 18/286) x 100 = 62.9%
2 marks: (c) The loss of some or all of the water of crystallisation by a hydrated salt when exposed to the atmosphere (e.g. Na2CO3.10H2O)
questions.explanation: Titres 25.40, 25.00, 24.95, 25.05 cm^3; average 25.00 cm^3. Moles of HCl = 0.100 x 25.00/1000 = 2.50 x 10^-3; moles of Na2CO3 in 25.0 cm^3 = 1.250 x 10^-3, so B = 0.0500 mol dm^-3. Molar mass = 14.3/0.0500 = 286 g mol^-1; 106 + 18x = 286 gives x = 10 (washing soda, Na2CO3.10H2O). Water = 180/286 x 100 = 62.9%. Washing soda is efflorescent: it loses water of crystallisation to the air.

questions.stem: A is 0.100 mol dm^-3 hydrochloric acid. B was prepared by dissolving 4.50 g of an impure sample of sodium hydroxide in distilled water and making the solution up to 1.00 dm^3. The impurity does not react with the acid. A was put in the burette and titrated against 25.0 cm^3 portions of B using phenolphthalein as indicator. The burette readings (cm^3) were: Rough: final 26.80, initial 0.00; 1st: final 26.40, initial 0.00; 2nd: final 26.35, initial 0.00; 3rd: final 26.45, initial 0.00. (a)(i) Tabulate the burette readings and calculate the volume of A used in each titration. [3 marks] (ii) Calculate the average volume of A used, from the three accurate titrations. [2 marks] (iii) State the colour change at the end-point. [1 mark] (iv) Write a balanced equation for the reaction. [1 mark] (b) From your results and the information provided, calculate the: (i) amount of HCl in the average titre; [2 marks] (ii) concentration of B in mol dm^-3; [2 marks] (iii) mass of pure NaOH in 1.00 dm^3 of B; [2 marks] (iv) percentage purity of the sodium hydroxide sample; [2 marks] (v) mass of impurity in 1.00 dm^3 of B. [1 mark] (c)(i) Why is sodium hydroxide not used as a primary standard? [2 marks] (ii) Name one suitable indicator other than phenolphthalein for this titration and give a reason. [2 marks] [H = 1.0, O = 16.0, Na = 23.0, Cl = 35.5]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Volumes of A (cm^3): rough 26.80; 26.40, 26.35, 26.45 (composite table with final, initial and volume rows, readings to 2 decimal places)
2 marks: (a)(ii) Average = (26.40 + 26.35 + 26.45)/3 = 26.40 cm^3
1 mark: (a)(iii) Pink to colourless
1 mark: (a)(iv) NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)
2 marks: (b)(i) 0.100 x 26.40/1000 = 2.64 x 10^-3 mol
2 marks: (b)(ii) mole ratio 1:1, so moles of NaOH = 2.64 x 10^-3 in 25.0 cm^3; concentration = 0.1056 mol dm^-3
2 marks: (b)(iii) 0.1056 x 40 = 4.22 g
2 marks: (b)(iv) % purity = 4.22/4.50 x 100 = 93.8%
1 mark: (b)(v) 4.50 - 4.22 = 0.28 g
2 marks: (c)(i) It is deliquescent (absorbs water from the air) and absorbs carbon(IV) oxide, so its mass cannot be weighed accurately and its concentration changes
2 marks: (c)(ii) Methyl orange (or methyl red) (1 mark); for a strong acid-strong base titration the pH changes sharply over a wide range (about 3 to 10) at the end-point, so either indicator changes colour at the equivalence point (1 mark)
questions.explanation: Titres 26.80, 26.40, 26.35, 26.45 cm^3; average 26.40 cm^3. Moles of HCl = 2.64 x 10^-3 = moles of NaOH in 25.0 cm^3 (1:1), so B = 0.1056 mol dm^-3 and contains 4.22 g pure NaOH per dm^3. Purity = 4.22/4.50 x 100 = 93.8%; impurity = 0.28 g. NaOH is deliquescent and absorbs CO2, so it is not a primary standard.

questions.stem: A is a solution containing 6.30 g of ethanedioic acid crystals, H2C2O4.2H2O, per dm^3. B is a solution containing 3.20 g of sodium hydroxide per dm^3. A was put in the burette and titrated against 25.0 cm^3 portions of B using phenolphthalein as indicator. The burette readings (cm^3) were: Rough: final 20.40, initial 0.00; 1st: final 20.00, initial 0.00; 2nd: final 20.45, initial 0.50; 3rd: final 20.05, initial 0.00. (a)(i) Tabulate the burette readings and calculate the volume of A used in each titration. [3 marks] (ii) Calculate the average volume of A used, from the three accurate titrations. [2 marks] (iii) State the colour change at the end-point. [1 mark] (b) From your results and the information provided, calculate the: (i) concentration of A in mol dm^-3; [2 marks] (ii) concentration of B in mol dm^-3; [2 marks] (iii) number of moles of A in the average titre; [2 marks] (iv) number of moles of B in 25.0 cm^3; [1 mark] (v) mole ratio of A to B in the reaction. [2 marks] (c)(i) Using your answer in (b)(v), write a balanced equation for the reaction. [2 marks] (ii) State the basicity of ethanedioic acid. [1 mark] (iii) Why is ethanedioic acid crystal suitable as a primary standard? [2 marks] [H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0, Na = 23.0]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Volumes of A (cm^3): rough 20.40; 20.00, 19.95, 20.05 (composite table with final, initial and volume rows, readings to 2 decimal places)
2 marks: (a)(ii) Average = (20.00 + 19.95 + 20.05)/3 = 20.00 cm^3
1 mark: (a)(iii) Pink to colourless
2 marks: (b)(i) Molar mass of H2C2O4.2H2O = 126 g mol^-1; 6.30/126 = 0.0500 mol dm^-3
2 marks: (b)(ii) 3.20/40 = 0.0800 mol dm^-3
2 marks: (b)(iii) 0.0500 x 20.00/1000 = 1.00 x 10^-3 mol
1 mark: (b)(iv) 0.0800 x 25.0/1000 = 2.00 x 10^-3 mol
2 marks: (b)(v) A : B = 1.00 x 10^-3 : 2.00 x 10^-3 = 1 : 2
2 marks: (c)(i) H2C2O4(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) -> Na2C2O4(aq) + 2H2O(l)
1 mark: (c)(ii) Two (dibasic)
2 marks: (c)(iii) Any two: it is obtainable in a pure state; it is stable in air (not deliquescent or efflorescent); it has a fairly high molar mass so weighing errors are small; it dissolves readily in water (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: Titres 20.40, 20.00, 19.95, 20.05 cm^3; average 20.00 cm^3. A = 6.30/126 = 0.0500 mol dm^-3; B = 3.20/40 = 0.0800 mol dm^-3. Moles of A used = 1.00 x 10^-3; moles of B in 25.0 cm^3 = 2.00 x 10^-3; ratio 1:2, so H2C2O4 + 2NaOH -> Na2C2O4 + 2H2O and the acid is dibasic. Ethanedioic acid crystals are pure, stable and of high molar mass, so they make a good primary standard.

questions.stem: A is 0.110 mol dm^-3 hydrochloric acid. B is a solution containing 6.90 g of a trioxocarbonate(IV) of a Group 1 metal, M2CO3, per dm^3. A was put in the burette and titrated against 25.0 cm^3 portions of B using methyl orange as indicator. The burette readings (cm^3) were: Rough: final 23.10, initial 0.00; 1st: final 22.70, initial 0.00; 2nd: final 22.75, initial 0.00; 3rd: final 22.75, initial 0.00. (a)(i) Tabulate the burette readings and calculate the volume of A used in each titration. [3 marks] (ii) Calculate the average volume of A used, from the three accurate titrations. [2 marks] (iii) State the colour change at the end-point. [1 mark] (b) The equation for the reaction is M2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2MCl + H2O + CO2. From your results and the information provided, calculate the: (i) amount of HCl in the average titre; [2 marks] (ii) concentration of B in mol dm^-3; [3 marks] (iii) molar mass of M2CO3; [2 marks] (iv) relative atomic mass of M, and identify M. [3 marks] (c)(i) A drop of B gave a lilac flame colour. Does this support your identification of M? [2 marks] (ii) State one source of error in a titration and how it may be avoided. [2 marks] [C = 12.0, O = 16.0]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Volumes of A (cm^3): rough 23.10; 22.70, 22.75, 22.75 (composite table with final, initial and volume rows, readings to 2 decimal places)
2 marks: (a)(ii) Average = (22.70 + 22.75 + 22.75)/3 = 22.73 cm^3
1 mark: (a)(iii) Yellow to orange
2 marks: (b)(i) 0.110 x 22.73/1000 = 2.500 x 10^-3 mol
3 marks: (b)(ii) Moles of M2CO3 = 2.500 x 10^-3/2 = 1.250 x 10^-3 mol in 25.0 cm^3 (2 marks); concentration = 0.0500 mol dm^-3 (1 mark)
2 marks: (b)(iii) Molar mass = 6.90/0.0500 = 138 g mol^-1
3 marks: (b)(iv) 2M + 60 = 138; M = 39 (2 marks); M is potassium (1 mark)
2 marks: (c)(i) Yes: a lilac flame is characteristic of potassium ions, which agrees with a relative atomic mass of 39
2 marks: (c)(ii) Any one: parallax in reading the burette - read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level; air bubble in the burette tip - expel before reading; over-shooting the end-point - add titrant dropwise near the end-point while swirling; dilution by wet apparatus - rinse with the solution to be used
questions.explanation: Titres 23.10, 22.70, 22.75, 22.75 cm^3; average 22.73 cm^3. Moles of HCl = 0.110 x 22.73/1000 = 2.500 x 10^-3; moles of M2CO3 in 25.0 cm^3 = 1.250 x 10^-3, so B = 0.0500 mol dm^-3. Molar mass = 6.90/0.0500 = 138 g mol^-1; 2M + 60 = 138 gives M = 39, potassium (K2CO3), confirmed by the lilac flame.

questions.stem: A was prepared by pipetting 10.0 cm^3 of a concentrated hydrochloric acid stock solution into a 250 cm^3 volumetric flask and making up to the mark with distilled water. B is a solution containing 4.00 g of sodium hydroxide per dm^3. A was put in the burette and titrated against 25.0 cm^3 portions of B using phenolphthalein as indicator. The burette readings (cm^3) were: Rough: final 21.20, initial 0.00; 1st: final 20.80, initial 0.00; 2nd: final 20.75, initial 0.00; 3rd: final 20.85, initial 0.00. (a)(i) Tabulate the burette readings and calculate the volume of A used in each titration. [3 marks] (ii) Calculate the average volume of A used, from the three accurate titrations. [2 marks] (iii) State the colour change at the end-point. [1 mark] (b) From your results and the information provided, calculate the: (i) concentration of B in mol dm^-3; [2 marks] (ii) concentration of A in mol dm^-3; [3 marks] (iii) concentration of the original stock acid in mol dm^-3; [3 marks] (iv) mass of sodium chloride formed in each titration. [2 marks] (c)(i) Describe briefly how the 250 cm^3 of A was made up accurately. [2 marks] (ii) What volume of the stock acid would be needed to prepare 500 cm^3 of 0.300 mol dm^-3 acid? [2 marks] [H = 1.0, O = 16.0, Na = 23.0, Cl = 35.5]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Volumes of A (cm^3): rough 21.20; 20.80, 20.75, 20.85 (composite table with final, initial and volume rows, readings to 2 decimal places)
2 marks: (a)(ii) Average = (20.80 + 20.75 + 20.85)/3 = 20.80 cm^3
1 mark: (a)(iii) Pink to colourless
2 marks: (b)(i) 4.00/40 = 0.100 mol dm^-3
3 marks: (b)(ii) Moles of NaOH = 0.100 x 25.0/1000 = 2.50 x 10^-3 = moles of HCl (1:1) (1 mark); concentration of A = 2.50 x 10^-3 x 1000/20.80 (1 mark) = 0.120 mol dm^-3 (1 mark)
3 marks: (b)(iii) C1V1 = C2V2: C1 x 10.0 = 0.120 x 250 (2 marks); C1 = 3.00 mol dm^-3 (1 mark) (dilution factor 25)
2 marks: (b)(iv) Moles of NaCl = 2.50 x 10^-3; mass = 2.50 x 10^-3 x 58.5 = 0.146 g
2 marks: (c)(i) The acid is run into the flask, distilled water added and mixed, then water added carefully (dropwise near the end) until the bottom of the meniscus is on the mark at eye level; the flask is stoppered and shaken/inverted to mix
2 marks: (c)(ii) V1 = C2V2/C1 = 0.300 x 500/3.00 = 50.0 cm^3
questions.explanation: Titres 21.20, 20.80, 20.75, 20.85 cm^3; average 20.80 cm^3. B = 4.00/40 = 0.100 mol dm^-3; 25.0 cm^3 contains 2.50 x 10^-3 mol NaOH, which reacts 1:1 with HCl, so A = 2.50 x 10^-3/(20.80/1000) = 0.120 mol dm^-3. The stock was diluted 25 times (10.0 cm^3 to 250 cm^3), so stock = 0.120 x 25 = 3.00 mol dm^-3. NaCl per titration = 2.50 x 10^-3 x 58.5 = 0.146 g. To make 500 cm^3 of 0.300 mol dm^-3: V = 0.300 x 500/3.00 = 50.0 cm^3.

questions.stem: B was prepared by dissolving 2.10 g of pure sodium hydrogentrioxocarbonate(IV), NaHCO3, in distilled water and making the solution up to 250 cm^3. A is a solution of hydrochloric acid. A was put in the burette and titrated against 25.0 cm^3 portions of B using methyl orange as indicator. The burette readings (cm^3) were: Rough: final 24.60, initial 0.00; 1st: final 24.20, initial 0.00; 2nd: final 24.15, initial 0.00; 3rd: final 24.25, initial 0.00. (a)(i) Tabulate the burette readings and calculate the volume of A used in each titration. [3 marks] (ii) Calculate the average volume of A used, from the three accurate titrations. [2 marks] (iii) State the colour change at the end-point. [1 mark] (b) Given that NaHCO3 + HCl -> NaCl + H2O + CO2, calculate the: (i) concentration of B in mol dm^-3; [3 marks] (ii) concentration of A in mol dm^-3; [3 marks] (iii) concentration of A in g dm^-3; [1 mark] (iv) volume of carbon(IV) oxide liberated at s.t.p. in each titration. [2 marks] (c)(i) What is a standard solution? [2 marks] (ii) State what would be observed if a few drops of A were added to solid NaHCO3, and give a test for the gas evolved. [3 marks] [H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0, Na = 23.0, Cl = 35.5; molar volume of a gas at s.t.p. = 22.4 dm^3]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Volumes of A (cm^3): rough 24.60; 24.20, 24.15, 24.25 (composite table with final, initial and volume rows, readings to 2 decimal places)
2 marks: (a)(ii) Average = (24.20 + 24.15 + 24.25)/3 = 24.20 cm^3
1 mark: (a)(iii) Yellow to orange
3 marks: (b)(i) Molar mass NaHCO3 = 84 g mol^-1 (1 mark); mass per dm^3 = 2.10 x 1000/250 = 8.40 g (1 mark); concentration = 8.40/84 = 0.100 mol dm^-3 (1 mark)
3 marks: (b)(ii) Moles of NaHCO3 = 0.100 x 25.0/1000 = 2.50 x 10^-3 = moles of HCl (1 mark); concentration = 2.50 x 10^-3 x 1000/24.20 (1 mark) = 0.103 mol dm^-3 (1 mark)
1 mark: (b)(iii) 0.103 x 36.5 = 3.76 g dm^-3
2 marks: (b)(iv) moles of CO2 = 2.50 x 10^-3; volume = 2.50 x 10^-3 x 22.4 = 0.0560 dm^3 (56.0 cm^3)
2 marks: (c)(i) A solution whose concentration is accurately known
3 marks: (c)(ii) Effervescence/brisk bubbling of a colourless, odourless gas (1 mark); the gas turns lime water milky (2 marks)
questions.explanation: Titres 24.60, 24.20, 24.15, 24.25 cm^3; average 24.20 cm^3. B contains 8.40 g NaHCO3 per dm^3 = 0.100 mol dm^-3; 25.0 cm^3 contains 2.50 x 10^-3 mol, reacting 1:1 with HCl. A = 2.50 x 10^-3/(24.20/1000) = 0.103 mol dm^-3 = 3.76 g dm^-3. CO2 = 2.50 x 10^-3 x 22.4 = 0.0560 dm^3. A standard solution has an accurately known concentration. Acid on NaHCO3 gives effervescence of CO2, which turns lime water milky.

questions.stem: C is a mixture of two salts. The following tests were carried out on C and the observations recorded. State the inference for each test. (a) C was shaken with distilled water and filtered. Observation: a white residue and a colourless filtrate were obtained. [1 mark] (b)(i) The residue was treated with dilute HNO3. Observation: effervescence; a colourless, odourless gas turned lime water milky; a clear solution remained. [2 marks] (ii) To a portion of the solution from (b)(i), NaOH(aq) was added in drops and then in excess. Observation: white gelatinous precipitate, soluble in excess. [2 marks] (iii) To another portion, NH3(aq) was added in drops and then in excess. Observation: white gelatinous precipitate, soluble in excess. [2 marks] (c)(i) A clean platinum wire dipped in the filtrate was held in a non-luminous flame. Observation: persistent golden-yellow flame. [2 marks] (ii) The filtrate was acidified with dilute HNO3 and AgNO3(aq) added, followed by excess NH3(aq). Observation: white precipitate which dissolved in excess NH3(aq). [3 marks] (d)(i) Name the two salts in C. [2 marks] (ii) Write an ionic equation for the formation of the precipitate in (c)(ii). [2 marks] (iii) Why was the filtrate acidified with dilute HNO3 before AgNO3(aq) was added? [2 marks] (iv) Write an equation for the reaction of the gas in (b)(i) with lime water. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) C contains one soluble and one insoluble salt
2 marks: (b)(i) Gas is CO2 (1 mark); CO3 2- present in residue (1 mark)
2 marks: (b)(ii) Zn2+, Al3+ or Pb2+ present
2 marks: (b)(iii) Zn2+ present (confirmed)
2 marks: (c)(i) Na+ present
3 marks: (c)(ii) Precipitate is AgCl (1 mark); Cl- present (2 marks)
2 marks: (d)(i) Zinc trioxocarbonate(IV), ZnCO3 (1 mark); sodium chloride, NaCl (1 mark)
2 marks: (d)(ii) Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> AgCl(s)
2 marks: (d)(iii) To remove (destroy) ions such as CO3 2- which would also give a white precipitate with Ag+
2 marks: (d)(iv) Ca(OH)2(aq) + CO2(g) -> CaCO3(s) + H2O(l)
questions.explanation: The insoluble residue fizzes with acid giving CO2, so it is a trioxocarbonate(IV); its cation gives a white precipitate soluble in excess of both NaOH and NH3, which is characteristic of Zn2+ (Al3+ and Pb2+ precipitates do not dissolve in excess NH3). The filtrate gives a golden-yellow flame (Na+) and a white precipitate with acidified AgNO3 that dissolves in NH3(aq) (AgCl, so Cl-). C is ZnCO3 + NaCl. HNO3 is added first to remove CO3 2- that would give a false white precipitate. Lime water turns milky because insoluble CaCO3 forms.

questions.stem: D is a pale green crystalline salt. The following tests were carried out on D. State the inference for each test. (a) A small amount of D was heated strongly in a dry test tube. Observation: colourless droplets condensed on the cooler part of the tube; the solid turned white and finally reddish-brown; a gas with a choking smell turned orange acidified K2Cr2O7 paper green. [3 marks] (b) D was dissolved in distilled water to give a pale green solution. (i) NaOH(aq) was added in drops and then in excess. Observation: dirty-green gelatinous precipitate, insoluble in excess, turning brown at the surface on standing. [2 marks] (ii) NH3(aq) was added in drops and then in excess. Observation: dirty-green precipitate, insoluble in excess. [1 mark] (iii) Dilute HCl and then BaCl2(aq) were added. Observation: white precipitate, insoluble in excess dilute HCl. [2 marks] (iv) A few drops of concentrated HNO3 were added to a portion, the mixture warmed, cooled and NaOH(aq) added in excess. Observation: reddish-brown precipitate, insoluble in excess. [2 marks] (c)(i) Identify D, including its water of crystallisation. [2 marks] (ii) Write an ionic equation for the formation of the precipitate in (b)(i). [2 marks] (iii) Explain why the precipitate in (b)(i) turned brown on standing. [2 marks] (iv) Why was dilute HCl added before BaCl2(aq) in (b)(iii)? [2 marks] (v) Name a reagent, other than NaOH(aq), that can be used to confirm Fe2+, and state the observation. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) D is a hydrated salt (water of crystallisation) (1 mark); gas is SO2 (1 mark); reddish-brown residue is Fe2O3, so D is likely an iron salt containing sulphur, e.g. a tetraoxosulphate(VI) (1 mark)
2 marks: (b)(i) Fe2+ present
1 mark: (b)(ii) Fe2+ confirmed
2 marks: (b)(iii) SO4 2- present
2 marks: (b)(iv) Fe2+ has been oxidised to Fe3+ by HNO3; Fe(OH)3 formed
2 marks: (c)(i) Iron(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) heptahydrate, FeSO4.7H2O (accept FeSO4.xH2O for 1 mark)
2 marks: (c)(ii) Fe2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) -> Fe(OH)2(s)
2 marks: (c)(iii) Iron(II) hydroxide is oxidised by atmospheric oxygen to brown iron(III) hydroxide
2 marks: (c)(iv) To remove CO3 2- and SO3 2- ions, which would also give white precipitates with Ba2+
2 marks: (c)(v) Potassium hexacyanoferrate(III) solution (1 mark); dark (Prussian/Turnbull's) blue precipitate (1 mark) (accept acidified KMnO4 decolourised)
questions.explanation: Heating gives water (hydrated salt), SO2 (turns dichromate green) and red-brown Fe2O3. The dirty-green precipitate insoluble in excess alkali is Fe(OH)2, showing Fe2+; it browns as air oxidises it to Fe(OH)3. The white precipitate with BaCl2 insoluble in HCl is BaSO4, showing SO4 2-. Concentrated HNO3 oxidises Fe2+ to Fe3+, giving reddish-brown Fe(OH)3 with NaOH. D is FeSO4.7H2O. HCl is added first so that CO3 2- or SO3 2- cannot give a false BaCO3/BaSO3 precipitate.

questions.stem: E is a blue crystalline salt. The following tests were carried out on E. State the inference for each test. (a) E was heated strongly in a dry test tube. Observation: brown gas evolved; a glowing splint was rekindled; black residue remained. [3 marks] (b) E was dissolved in distilled water to give a blue solution. (i) NaOH(aq) was added in drops and then in excess. Observation: pale blue precipitate, insoluble in excess. [2 marks] (ii) NH3(aq) was added in drops and then in excess. Observation: pale blue precipitate which dissolved in excess to give a deep blue solution. [2 marks] (iii) Freshly prepared FeSO4(aq) was added to a portion, and concentrated H2SO4 was carefully poured down the side of the inclined tube. Observation: a brown ring formed at the junction of the two liquids. [2 marks] (iv) A clean iron nail was placed in a portion of the solution for some minutes. Observation: a reddish-brown deposit formed on the nail and the blue colour of the solution faded. [2 marks] (c)(i) Identify E. [1 mark] (ii) Write a balanced equation for the action of heat on E. [3 marks] (iii) Name the species responsible for the deep blue colour in (b)(ii). [2 marks] (iv) Write an ionic equation for the reaction in (b)(iv). [2 marks] (v) Why must the concentrated H2SO4 in (b)(iii) be added carefully down the side of the tube? [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Brown gas is NO2 (1 mark); gas rekindling splint is O2 (1 mark); NO3- of a heavy metal present; black residue may be CuO (1 mark)
2 marks: (b)(i) Cu2+ present
2 marks: (b)(ii) Cu2+ confirmed
2 marks: (b)(iii) NO3- present
2 marks: (b)(iv) Copper displaced by iron; iron is more reactive (electropositive) than copper
1 mark: (c)(i) Copper(II) trioxonitrate(V), Cu(NO3)2
3 marks: (c)(ii) 2Cu(NO3)2 -> 2CuO + 4NO2 + O2 (1 mark products, 2 marks balanced)
2 marks: (c)(iii) Tetraamminecopper(II) ion, [Cu(NH3)4]2+
2 marks: (c)(iv) Fe(s) + Cu2+(aq) -> Fe2+(aq) + Cu(s)
1 mark: (c)(v) So that the dense acid forms a separate lower layer (and to avoid violent heating/splashing), allowing the ring to form at the junction
questions.explanation: Brown NO2 and O2 with a black CuO residue show a heavy-metal trioxonitrate(V). A pale blue precipitate insoluble in excess NaOH but dissolving in excess NH3 to a deep blue solution ([Cu(NH3)4]2+) confirms Cu2+. The brown ring test confirms NO3-. Iron displaces copper (reddish-brown deposit) because it is higher in the activity series. E is Cu(NO3)2: 2Cu(NO3)2 -> 2CuO + 4NO2 + O2.

questions.stem: F is a white crystalline salt. The following tests were carried out on F. State the inference for each test. (a) F was heated gently in a dry test tube. Observation: white fumes; a white sublimate formed on the cooler part of the tube; no residue remained. [2 marks] (b) F was warmed with NaOH(aq). Observation: a colourless gas with a pungent smell turned moist red litmus paper blue and formed dense white fumes with a glass rod dipped in concentrated HCl. [3 marks] (c) A solution of F was acidified with dilute HNO3 and AgNO3(aq) added. Observation: white precipitate, soluble in excess NH3(aq). [2 marks] (d) F was warmed with concentrated H2SO4. Observation: steamy fumes which turned moist blue litmus paper red and gave dense white fumes with ammonia. [2 marks] (e)(i) Identify F. [1 mark] (ii) Write a balanced equation for the reaction in (b). [2 marks] (iii) Explain why the change in (a) is not true sublimation. [2 marks] (iv) Why is the gas evolved in (b) dried with calcium oxide and not with concentrated H2SO4? [2 marks] (v) State how the gas in (b) is collected in the laboratory and give a reason. [2 marks] (vi) State two uses of F. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) F sublimes/dissociates on heating; F may be an ammonium salt
3 marks: (b) Gas is NH3 (2 marks); NH4+ present (1 mark)
2 marks: (c) Cl- present
2 marks: (d) Gas is HCl; Cl- confirmed
1 mark: (e)(i) Ammonium chloride, NH4Cl
2 marks: (e)(ii) NH4Cl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O + NH3
2 marks: (e)(iii) NH4Cl dissociates into NH3 and HCl on heating; the gases recombine on the cooler part (thermal dissociation, a chemical change), whereas true sublimation is a physical change of the same substance
2 marks: (e)(iv) NH3 is basic and reacts with concentrated H2SO4 (to form ammonium tetraoxosulphate(VI)); CaO is basic and does not react with it
2 marks: (e)(v) By upward delivery (downward displacement of air) (1 mark) because NH3 is less dense than air and very soluble in water (1 mark)
2 marks: (e)(vi) Any two: electrolyte in dry (Leclanche) cells; flux in soldering/galvanising; nitrogenous fertiliser; in medicine (expectorant) (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: F sublimes without residue and gives NH3 (alkaline gas, white fumes of NH4Cl with HCl) when warmed with alkali, so NH4+ is present. The white precipitate with acidified AgNO3 soluble in NH3 shows Cl-, confirmed by steamy HCl fumes with conc. H2SO4. F is NH4Cl: NH4Cl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O + NH3. Its "sublimation" is really dissociation into NH3 and HCl followed by recombination. Ammonia is dried with CaO since it reacts with acidic drying agents, and is collected by upward delivery because it is lighter than air and very soluble in water.

questions.stem: G and H are two white salts. Solutions of each were tested as below. State the inference for each test. (a) NaOH(aq) was added in drops and then in excess to each. Observation: G and H each gave a white precipitate, soluble in excess. [2 marks] (b) NH3(aq) was added in drops and then in excess to each. Observation: G and H each gave a white precipitate, insoluble in excess. [2 marks] (c) Dilute HCl was added to each. Observation: G gave a white precipitate which dissolved on warming and reappeared on cooling; H gave no visible change. [2 marks] (d) KI(aq) was added to each. Observation: G gave a yellow precipitate; H gave no visible change. [2 marks] (e) Solid G was heated strongly. Observation: crackling sound; brown gas evolved; a glowing splint was rekindled; the residue was reddish-brown when hot and yellow when cold. [2 marks] (f) Dilute HCl followed by BaCl2(aq) was added to the solution of H. Observation: white precipitate, insoluble in excess acid. [2 marks] (g)(i) Identify G and H. [2 marks] (ii) Write an ionic equation for the reaction in (d). [2 marks] (iii) Explain why NaOH(aq) alone cannot distinguish between the cations in G and H. [2 marks] (iv) Name the soluble species formed when excess NaOH(aq) is added to the precipitate from H. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Zn2+, Al3+ or Pb2+ present in each
2 marks: (b) Al3+ or Pb2+ present in each (Zn2+ absent)
2 marks: (c) G: Pb2+ present (PbCl2 soluble in hot water) (1 mark); H: Pb2+ absent, so H contains Al3+ (1 mark)
2 marks: (d) G: Pb2+ confirmed (PbI2) (1 mark); H: Pb2+ absent (1 mark)
2 marks: (e) NO2 and O2 evolved; G is a trioxonitrate(V) (1 mark); residue is PbO, confirming Pb2+ (1 mark)
2 marks: (f) SO4 2- present in H
2 marks: (g)(i) G is lead(II) trioxonitrate(V), Pb(NO3)2 (1 mark); H is aluminium tetraoxosulphate(VI), Al2(SO4)3 (1 mark)
2 marks: (g)(ii) Pb2+(aq) + 2I-(aq) -> PbI2(s)
2 marks: (g)(iii) Both Pb(OH)2 and Al(OH)3 are amphoteric, so both precipitates are white and dissolve in excess NaOH(aq)
2 marks: (g)(iv) Tetrahydroxoaluminate(III) ion, [Al(OH)4]- (aluminate)
questions.explanation: Both cations give white amphoteric hydroxides soluble in excess NaOH but insoluble in excess NH3, so each is Pb2+ or Al3+. Only G gives PbCl2 (soluble in hot water) with HCl and yellow PbI2 with KI, so G contains Pb2+; heating G gives NO2, O2 and PbO (red-brown hot, yellow cold), so G is Pb(NO3)2. H contains Al3+, and BaSO4 forms with BaCl2, so H is Al2(SO4)3. Excess NaOH dissolves Al(OH)3 as [Al(OH)4]-.

questions.stem: J is a white solid. The following tests were carried out on J. State the inference for each test. (a) J was shaken with distilled water. Observation: J did not dissolve. [1 mark] (b) J was treated with dilute HCl. Observation: effervescence; a colourless, odourless gas turned lime water milky; a clear colourless solution remained. [2 marks] (c) A platinum wire dipped in the solution from (b) was held in a non-luminous flame. Observation: brick-red flame. [2 marks] (d) NaOH(aq) was added in drops and then in excess to a portion of the solution from (b). Observation: white precipitate, insoluble in excess. [2 marks] (e) NH3(aq) was added in drops and then in excess to another portion. Observation: no precipitate. [2 marks] (f) Ammonium ethanedioate solution was added to a third portion. Observation: white precipitate. [1 mark] (g) Solid J was heated very strongly for some time and allowed to cool. A few drops of water were added to the residue. Observation: the residue hissed, became hot and crumbled to a powder; its solution turned red litmus blue. [3 marks] (h)(i) Identify J. [1 mark] (ii) Write a balanced equation for the action of heat on J. [2 marks] (iii) Write a balanced equation for the reaction that makes lime water milky. [2 marks] (iv) Explain why the milkiness disappears when the gas in (b) is passed into the lime water for a long time. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) J is an insoluble salt
2 marks: (b) Gas is CO2 (1 mark); CO3 2- present (1 mark)
2 marks: (c) Ca2+ present
2 marks: (d) Ca2+ or Mg2+ present
2 marks: (e) Ca2+ present (Mg2+, Zn2+, Al3+ and Pb2+ absent)
1 mark: (f) Ca2+ confirmed (calcium ethanedioate)
3 marks: (g) Residue is calcium oxide (quicklime) (1 mark); slaking is exothermic, forming Ca(OH)2 (1 mark); the solution is alkaline (1 mark)
1 mark: (h)(i) Calcium trioxocarbonate(IV), CaCO3
2 marks: (h)(ii) CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)
2 marks: (h)(iii) Ca(OH)2(aq) + CO2(g) -> CaCO3(s) + H2O(l)
2 marks: (h)(iv) Excess CO2 converts the insoluble CaCO3 into soluble calcium hydrogentrioxocarbonate(IV): CaCO3 + H2O + CO2 -> Ca(HCO3)2
questions.explanation: J is insoluble and fizzes with dilute acid giving CO2, so it is a trioxocarbonate(IV). The brick-red flame, a white precipitate with NaOH insoluble in excess, no precipitate with NH3 and a white precipitate with ammonium ethanedioate all identify Ca2+. Strong heating gives quicklime, which slakes exothermically to alkaline Ca(OH)2. J is CaCO3: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Lime water turns milky (CaCO3) and clears again with excess CO2 as soluble Ca(HCO3)2 forms.

questions.stem: K is a white salt that is soluble in water. The following tests were carried out on K. State the inference for each test. (a) A clean platinum wire moistened with concentrated HCl and dipped in K was held in a non-luminous flame. Observation: persistent golden-yellow flame. [2 marks] (b) K was warmed with dilute HCl. Observation: a colourless gas with a choking smell was evolved; it turned filter paper soaked in acidified K2Cr2O7 from orange to green. [3 marks] (c) BaCl2(aq) was added to a solution of K, and then dilute HCl was added to the mixture. Observation: white precipitate which dissolved in the dilute HCl with evolution of a gas with a choking smell. [3 marks] (d) A solution of K was warmed with NaOH(aq). Observation: no precipitate; no gas evolved. [2 marks] (e) A few drops of acidified KMnO4 were added to a solution of K. Observation: the purple colour was discharged. [2 marks] (f)(i) Identify K. [1 mark] (ii) Write an ionic equation for the reaction in (b). [2 marks] (iii) What property of the gas in (b) is shown by its effect on acidified K2Cr2O7? [2 marks] (iv) Describe a test that distinguishes the gas in (b) from hydrogen sulphide. [2 marks] (v) State one harmful effect of the gas in (b) on the environment. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Na+ present
3 marks: (b) Gas is SO2 (2 marks); SO3 2- present (1 mark)
3 marks: (c) Precipitate is BaSO3 (1 mark); SO3 2- confirmed (1 mark); SO4 2- absent (1 mark)
2 marks: (d) No heavy-metal cation present (1 mark); NH4+ absent (1 mark)
2 marks: (e) K is a reducing agent; SO3 2- confirmed
1 mark: (f)(i) Sodium trioxosulphate(IV) (sodium sulphite), Na2SO3
2 marks: (f)(ii) SO3 2-(aq) + 2H+(aq) -> SO2(g) + H2O(l)
2 marks: (f)(iii) SO2 is a reducing agent: it reduces orange Cr2O7 2- to green Cr3+
2 marks: (f)(iv) Lead(II) ethanoate paper: H2S turns it black (PbS), SO2 has no effect (accept smell: H2S smells of rotten eggs)
1 mark: (f)(v) Any one: causes acid rain; damages plants/buildings; respiratory irritation
questions.explanation: The golden-yellow flame shows Na+. A choking gas that turns acidified dichromate green is SO2 (a reducing agent), so SO3 2- is present; the white BaSO3 precipitate dissolves in acid releasing SO2, ruling out SO4 2-. No precipitate or ammonia with NaOH rules out heavy-metal and NH4+ ions, and decolourised KMnO4 shows a reducing anion. K is Na2SO3: SO3 2- + 2H+ -> SO2 + H2O. H2S, unlike SO2, blackens lead(II) ethanoate paper. SO2 causes acid rain.

questions.stem: L, M and N are organic compounds. The following tests were carried out. State the inference for each test. (a) L is a colourless liquid with a vinegar-like smell. (i) L was added to solid NaHCO3. Observation: effervescence; a colourless gas turned lime water milky. [2 marks] (ii) L was warmed with ethanol and a few drops of concentrated H2SO4, then poured into water. Observation: a sweet, fruity smell. [2 marks] (iii) Moist blue litmus paper was dipped in L. Observation: the paper turned red. [1 mark] (b) M is a white crystalline solid that dissolves readily in water. (i) A solution of M was warmed with Fehling's solution (or Benedict's solution). Observation: a brick-red precipitate. [2 marks] (ii) Iodine solution was added to a solution of M. Observation: no blue-black colour. [1 mark] (c) N is a colourless gas. (i) N was bubbled into bromine water. Observation: the red-brown colour was rapidly discharged. [2 marks] (ii) N was bubbled into acidified KMnO4. Observation: the purple colour was discharged. [1 mark] (d)(i) Name the functional group in L and the class of compound formed in (a)(ii). [2 marks] (ii) Suggest a name for M. [1 mark] (iii) Write a balanced equation for the reaction of ethanoic acid with NaHCO3. [2 marks] (iv) Given that N has two carbon atoms, write an equation for its reaction with bromine. [2 marks] (v) State the role of the concentrated H2SO4 in (a)(ii). [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) CO2 evolved; L is acidic / contains -COOH (alkanoic acid)
2 marks: (a)(ii) An ester (alkanoate) is formed; L is an alkanoic acid
1 mark: (a)(iii) L is acidic
2 marks: (b)(i) M is a reducing sugar
1 mark: (b)(ii) Starch absent
2 marks: (c)(i) N is unsaturated (contains C=C or C triple bond C)
1 mark: (c)(ii) Unsaturation confirmed
2 marks: (d)(i) Carboxyl group, -COOH (1 mark); ester/alkanoate (1 mark)
1 mark: (d)(ii) Glucose (accept fructose/maltose)
2 marks: (d)(iii) CH3COOH + NaHCO3 -> CH3COONa + H2O + CO2
2 marks: (d)(iv) CH2=CH2 + Br2 -> CH2BrCH2Br (1,2-dibromoethane)
2 marks: (d)(v) It acts as a catalyst and as a dehydrating agent, removing water and shifting the equilibrium towards the ester
questions.explanation: L liberates CO2 from NaHCO3, turns blue litmus red and forms a fruity ester with ethanol, so it is an alkanoic acid (-COOH), e.g. ethanoic acid. M reduces Fehling's/Benedict's solution to brick-red Cu2O and gives no blue-black colour with iodine, so it is a reducing sugar such as glucose and not starch. N decolourises bromine water and acidified KMnO4, so it is unsaturated; with two carbons it is ethene: CH2=CH2 + Br2 -> CH2BrCH2Br. Concentrated H2SO4 catalyses esterification and removes water.

questions.stem: A spot of a black ink X and spots of two pure dyes A and B were placed on a pencil line 1.5 cm from the bottom of a strip of chromatography paper. The strip was stood in a solvent whose level was below the line. When the solvent front had moved 12.0 cm above the line, the paper was removed and dried. X gave three spots at distances of 3.0 cm, 6.6 cm, 9.6 cm from the line; A gave one spot at 6.6 cm and B one spot at 4.2 cm. (a) Calculate the Rf value of each spot from X. [3 marks] (b) Which of the dyes A and B is present in X? Give a reason. [1 mark] (c) How many components does X contain? [1 mark] (d) Why was the starting line drawn in pencil and not in ink? [1 mark] (e) Why must the solvent level be below the starting line? [1 mark] (f) Explain why the components of X separate. [2 marks] (g) State one other application of chromatography. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Rf = distance moved by spot/distance moved by solvent: 3.0/12.0 = 0.25; 6.6/12.0 = 0.55; 9.6/12.0 = 0.80
1 mark: (b) A: its Rf (6.6/12.0 = 0.55) matches that of the middle spot of X; B (Rf 0.35) matches none
1 mark: (c) Three
1 mark: (d) Pencil (graphite) does not dissolve in the solvent and move up with it, whereas ink would
1 mark: (e) Otherwise the spots would dissolve into the solvent in the beaker instead of moving up the paper
2 marks: (f) The components have different solubilities in the solvent and different degrees of adsorption onto the paper (1 mark), so they move up the paper at different rates (1 mark)
1 mark: (g) Any one: separating plant pigments/chlorophyll; detecting food colourings or drugs; identifying amino acids/sugars; forensic analysis
questions.explanation: Rf values: 0.25, 0.55, 0.80. Dye A has Rf 0.55, the same as the middle spot, so A is in X; B (Rf 0.35) is not. X has three components. Pencil is used because it does not dissolve in the solvent, and the line must be above the solvent so the spots are not washed into it. Components separate because they differ in solubility in the solvent and in adsorption on the paper.

questions.stem: 0.048 g of magnesium ribbon was added to excess dilute hydrochloric acid in a flask connected to a gas syringe. The volume V of hydrogen collected at room temperature was recorded at intervals: t/s: 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 210; V/cm^3: 0, 20, 33, 41, 46, 48, 48, 48. (a) Calculate the average rate of reaction, in cm^3 s^-1, (i) during the first 30 s and (ii) between 60 s and 90 s. [3 marks] (b) Explain why the rate decreases as the reaction proceeds. [2 marks] (c) At what time did the reaction stop? [1 mark] (d) Calculate the volume of hydrogen expected from 0.048 g of magnesium. [Mg = 24; molar volume of a gas at room temperature = 24.0 dm^3] [2 marks] (e) State and explain the effect on the initial rate of using the same mass of magnesium powder instead of ribbon. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) 20/30 = 0.67 cm^3 s^-1 (1.5 marks); (ii) (41 - 33)/30 = 0.27 cm^3 s^-1 (1.5 marks)
2 marks: (b) The concentration of acid (and surface area of magnesium) falls as reactants are used up, so there are fewer effective collisions per second
1 mark: (c) At about 150 s (the volume stays constant at 48 cm^3)
2 marks: (d) Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2; moles Mg = 0.048/24 = 0.0020 mol = moles H2 (1 mark); volume = 0.0020 x 24 000 = 48 cm^3 (1 mark)
2 marks: (e) The initial rate increases (1 mark) because the powder has a larger surface area exposed to the acid, giving more frequent collisions (1 mark)
questions.explanation: Average rate in the first 30 s = 20/30 = 0.67 cm^3 s^-1; between 60 s and 90 s = 8/30 = 0.27 cm^3 s^-1. The rate falls because the reactants are being used up, so collisions become less frequent. The reaction stops at about 150 s. Moles of Mg = 0.048/24 = 0.0020 mol, giving 0.0020 mol H2 = 48 cm^3, which matches the final reading. Powdered Mg reacts faster because of its larger surface area.

questions.stem: A student determined the maximum mass of potassium trioxonitrate(V), KNO3, that dissolves in 50.0 g of water at different temperatures: temperature/degrees C: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60; mass of KNO3/g: 15.80, 22.90, 31.95, 42.75, 55.00. (a) Calculate the solubility of KNO3 in g per 100 g of water at each temperature. [2 marks] (b) A saturated solution of KNO3 in 100 g of water at 60 degrees C is cooled to 30 degrees C. Calculate the mass of crystals deposited. [2 marks] (c) Define solubility. [2 marks] (d) State how temperature affects the solubility of (i) KNO3 and (ii) gases in water. [2 marks] (e) Name the separation technique that makes use of differences in solubility with temperature. [1 mark] (f) State one precaution taken in the experiment. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Solubility = mass x 100/50: 31.6, 45.8, 63.9, 85.5, 110.0 g per 100 g water
2 marks: (b) 110.0 - 45.8 = 64.2 g
2 marks: (c) The maximum mass (or amount) of solute that will dissolve in 100 g (or 1 dm^3) of solvent at a given temperature to form a saturated solution
2 marks: (d)(i) Solubility of KNO3 increases with temperature (1 mark); (ii) solubility of gases decreases as temperature rises (1 mark)
1 mark: (e) Fractional crystallisation
1 mark: (f) Any one: temperature kept constant while dissolving; solution stirred until no more dissolves; undissolved solid filtered off before weighing; evaporating dish dried to constant mass
questions.explanation: Doubling each mass gives solubilities of 31.6, 45.8, 63.9, 85.5, 110.0 g per 100 g water. Cooling a saturated solution from 60 to 30 degrees C deposits 110.0 - 45.8 = 64.2 g of crystals. The solubility of KNO3 rises steeply with temperature, while that of gases falls; fractional crystallisation exploits such differences.

questions.stem: 50.0 cm^3 of 1.00 mol dm^-3 hydrochloric acid and 50.0 cm^3 of 1.00 mol dm^-3 sodium hydroxide solution, both at 28.0 degrees C, were mixed in a plastic (polystyrene) cup and stirred. The highest temperature reached was 34.7 degrees C. [specific heat capacity of solution = 4.2 J g^-1 K^-1; density of solution = 1.0 g cm^-3] (a) Calculate the rise in temperature. [1 mark] (b) Calculate the heat evolved in the reaction. [2 marks] (c) Calculate the number of moles of water formed. [2 marks] (d) Calculate the enthalpy of neutralisation, with its sign. [2 marks] (e) Explain why the value obtained using ethanoic acid instead of hydrochloric acid would be numerically smaller. [2 marks] (f) State one assumption made in the calculation. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) 34.7 - 28.0 = 6.7 K
2 marks: (b) Heat = mc(delta T) = 100 x 4.2 x 6.7 = 2814 J
2 marks: (c) Moles of HCl = moles of NaOH = 1.00 x 50.0/1000 = 0.0500 mol; H+ + OH- -> H2O, so 0.0500 mol water
2 marks: (d) delta H = -2814/0.0500 = -56280 J mol^-1 = -56.3 kJ mol^-1 (1 mark value, 1 mark negative sign)
2 marks: (e) Ethanoic acid is a weak acid, only partially ionised; some of the heat released is used to ionise it completely (bond breaking absorbs energy)
1 mark: (f) Any one: no heat lost to the surroundings/cup; solution has the same specific heat capacity and density as water; heat capacity of the cup is negligible
questions.explanation: Temperature rise = 6.7 K. Mass of solution = 100 g, so heat = 100 x 4.2 x 6.7 = 2814 J. 0.0500 mol of water is formed, so delta H = -2814/0.0500 = -56.3 kJ mol^-1 (the accepted value for a strong acid and strong base is about -57 kJ mol^-1). A weak acid gives a smaller value because energy is absorbed in ionising it.

questions.stem: Copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) solution was electrolysed using copper electrodes, with a steady current of 0.50 A for 40 minutes. The results were: mass of cathode before = 12.46 g, after = 12.86 g; mass of anode before = 12.80 g, after = 12.41 g. (a) Calculate the change in mass of each electrode. [2 marks] (b) Calculate the quantity of electricity passed. [1 mark] (c) Use the change in mass of the cathode to estimate the value of the Faraday constant. [Cu = 63.5] [3 marks] (d) Write the half-equations for the reactions at the anode and at the cathode. [2 marks] (e) Explain why the blue colour of the electrolyte does not fade. [1 mark] (f) State one industrial application of this process. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Cathode gains 12.86 - 12.46 = 0.40 g (1 mark); anode loses 12.80 - 12.41 = 0.39 g (1 mark)
1 mark: (b) Q = It = 0.50 x 40 x 60 = 1200 C
3 marks: (c) Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu: 2 mol of electrons deposit 63.5 g (1 mark); 2F = 1200 x 63.5/0.40 (1 mark); F = 95250 C mol^-1 (about 9.5 x 10^4) (1 mark)
2 marks: (d) Anode: Cu(s) -> Cu2+(aq) + 2e- (1 mark); cathode: Cu2+(aq) + 2e- -> Cu(s) (1 mark)
1 mark: (e) Copper(II) ions removed at the cathode are replaced by copper(II) ions formed at the anode, so their concentration stays constant
1 mark: (f) Any one: purification (refining) of copper; electroplating with copper
questions.explanation: The cathode gains 0.40 g and the anode loses 0.39 g. Q = 0.50 x 2400 = 1200 C. Since 2 faradays deposit 63.5 g of copper, F = 1200 x 63.5/(2 x 0.40) = 95250 C mol^-1, close to the accepted 96 500 C mol^-1. The copper anode dissolves (Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e-) as copper deposits on the cathode (Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu), so [Cu2+] and the blue colour stay constant. This is used to refine copper and in electroplating.

questions.stem: In the preparation of copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) crystals, black copper(II) oxide was added in small portions, with warming and stirring, to 50.0 cm^3 of 1.00 mol dm^-3 tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid until some solid remained undissolved. The mixture was filtered and the filtrate treated to obtain 10.0 g of dry blue crystals of CuSO4.5H2O. [H = 1.0, O = 16.0, S = 32.0, Cu = 63.5] (a) Why was copper(II) oxide added in excess? [1 mark] (b) How did the student know that the oxide was in excess? [1 mark] (c) Describe how the crystals were obtained from the filtrate. [2 marks] (d) Write a balanced equation for the reaction. [2 marks] (e) Calculate the theoretical mass of CuSO4.5H2O that could be obtained. [2 marks] (f) Calculate the percentage yield. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) To ensure that all the acid is used up (neutralised), so the salt is not contaminated with acid
1 mark: (b) Some black solid remained undissolved
2 marks: (c) The filtrate was evaporated/heated to concentrate it to saturation (crystallisation point) and allowed to cool slowly so crystals formed (1 mark); the crystals were filtered off, washed with a little cold distilled water and dried between filter papers (1 mark)
2 marks: (d) CuO(s) + H2SO4(aq) -> CuSO4(aq) + H2O(l)
2 marks: (e) Moles of H2SO4 = 1.00 x 50.0/1000 = 0.0500 mol = moles of CuSO4.5H2O (1 mark); molar mass = 249.5 g mol^-1, mass = 0.0500 x 249.5 = 12.48 g (1 mark)
2 marks: (f) % yield = 10.0/12.48 x 100 = 80.2%
questions.explanation: Excess CuO ensures all the acid reacts; undissolved black solid shows the excess. The filtrate is concentrated, cooled to crystallise, and the crystals filtered and dried between filter papers. CuO + H2SO4 -> CuSO4 + H2O. 0.0500 mol of acid gives 0.0500 mol of CuSO4.5H2O (molar mass 249.5), i.e. 12.48 g. Percentage yield = 10.0/12.48 x 100 = 80.2%.

questions.stem: Soap solution was run from a burette into 50.0 cm^3 portions of water samples, with shaking, until a permanent lather formed. Each sample was tested before and after boiling (and cooling). Volumes of soap solution used (cm^3): distilled water: unboiled 0.5, boiled 0.5; P: unboiled 12.5, boiled 0.5; Q: unboiled 10.5, boiled 10.5; R: unboiled 8.0, boiled 4.5. (a) Which sample contains (i) only temporary hardness, (ii) only permanent hardness, (iii) both? [3 marks] (b) Why was distilled water also tested? [1 mark] (c) Calculate the volume of soap solution used up by the temporary hardness in 50.0 cm^3 of R. [1 mark] (d) Write a balanced equation to show how boiling removes temporary hardness. [2 marks] (e) Name a substance that removes permanent hardness and write an ionic equation for its action. [2 marks] (f) State one advantage of hard water. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) P (1 mark); (ii) Q (1 mark); (iii) R (1 mark)
1 mark: (b) As a control: it shows the volume of soap needed to form a lather with water containing no hardness
1 mark: (c) 8.0 - 4.5 = 3.5 cm^3
2 marks: (d) Ca(HCO3)2(aq) -> CaCO3(s) + H2O(l) + CO2(g) (accept the Mg(HCO3)2 equation)
2 marks: (e) Washing soda, Na2CO3.10H2O (accept ion-exchange resin/permutit) (1 mark); Ca2+(aq) + CO3 2-(aq) -> CaCO3(s) (1 mark)
1 mark: (f) Any one: provides calcium for bones and teeth; pleasant taste; does not dissolve lead from pipes; useful in brewing
questions.explanation: P needs 12.5 cm^3 before boiling but only as much as distilled water after, so its hardness is all temporary. Q needs the same volume before and after boiling, so it is permanently hard. R needs less after boiling but still more than distilled water, so it has both. Distilled water is the control. In R, temporary hardness used 8.0 - 4.5 = 3.5 cm^3 of soap. Boiling decomposes Ca(HCO3)2 to insoluble CaCO3; washing soda precipitates Ca2+ as CaCO3. Hard water supplies calcium for bones and teeth.

questions.stem: Five solutions S1 to S5, each of concentration 0.1 mol dm^-3, were tested with universal indicator. Results: S1: red, pH 1; S2: orange-yellow, pH 5; S3: green, pH 7; S4: blue, pH 9; S5: violet, pH 13. (a) Classify each solution as strongly acidic, weakly acidic, neutral, weakly alkaline or strongly alkaline. [3 marks] (b) Suggest one possible identity for each of S1 and S5 from: aqueous ammonia, hydrochloric acid, sodium chloride, sodium hydroxide, ethanoic acid. [1 mark] (c) Calculate the pH of 0.010 mol dm^-3 hydrochloric acid. [2 marks] (d) Calculate the pH of 0.0010 mol dm^-3 sodium hydroxide solution. [2 marks] (e) Which of the solutions would liberate carbon(IV) oxide from sodium trioxocarbonate(IV)? [1 mark] (f) State one advantage of a pH meter over universal indicator. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) S1 strongly acidic; S2 weakly acidic; S3 neutral; S4 weakly alkaline; S5 strongly alkaline (deduct 1 mark for each error, to a minimum of 0)
1 mark: (b) S1 hydrochloric acid; S5 sodium hydroxide (both needed)
2 marks: (c) [H+] = 0.010 = 10^-2 mol dm^-3 (1 mark); pH = -log10[H+] = 2 (1 mark)
2 marks: (d) [OH-] = 10^-3, pOH = 3 (1 mark); pH = 14 - 3 = 11 (1 mark)
1 mark: (e) S1 and S2 (the acidic solutions)
1 mark: (f) It gives a more precise (numerical) reading and is not affected by the colour of the solution
questions.explanation: pH below 7 is acidic (S1 strong, S2 weak), 7 is neutral (S3), above 7 alkaline (S4 weak, S5 strong). S1 could be HCl and S5 NaOH (S2 ethanoic acid, S3 NaCl, S4 ammonia). For 0.010 mol dm^-3 HCl, pH = -log(10^-2) = 2. For 0.0010 mol dm^-3 NaOH, pOH = 3 and pH = 11. The acidic solutions S1 and S2 release CO2 from a trioxocarbonate(IV). A pH meter gives a precise reading.
